hook: Disks die at a steady, predictable rate. So why is a dead disk the least scary thing in storage?
title: Dead disks are the easy problem in storage
body:
Storage makes one promise that outranks speed, cost and features: the bytes you write come back unchanged. A slow photo service annoys users. A service that loses photos loses them forever.

You might expect dying disks to be the main threat. They are the easy part, because a dead disk is loud and the system repairs it. The real losses come from **silent corruption**, software bugs, and humans or tools deleting the wrong thing.
takeaway: Loud failures get repaired. Quiet ones get replicated.
deeper:
**One app, five answers:** Take a global app with 1 billion users. It stores profiles, photos and videos, messages, logs, and an analytics lake. Each needs a different answer to "how safe is safe enough?" Profiles are small and needed to log in. Messages are write-heavy. Photos are huge blobs. Logs can often be re-derived. Analytics users can wait hours.

**Why disks are easy:** Drive failure is frequent but noisy. The system notices, rebuilds the missing copy from the others, and moves on. Redundancy was designed for exactly this.

**Why the rest is hard:** A flipped bit raises no alarm. A bug ships to every server at once. A mistaken delete is, to the storage system, a valid request, and replication applies it everywhere. Across six major public incidents (S3 2017, GitLab 2017, Azure 2014, DynamoDB 2015, UniSuper 2024, Google 2015), none was caused by too many disks failing at random.

quiz.q: Your storage vendor boasts that its replicas survive any two simultaneous disk failures. Name two ways you could still lose data.
quiz.a: Silent corruption that gets replicated to every copy, a software bug shipped to all servers, or a mistaken delete that replication applies everywhere. Redundancy only answers hardware loss.

mcq.q: Which kind of failure do replicated storage systems handle most easily?
options: A single drive dying outright
A bit flipping silently on disk
An engineer deleting the wrong table
A buggy deploy reaching every server
mcq.why: A dead drive is loud: the system detects it and rebuilds from surviving copies. The others raise no error or hit every copy at once.

hook: Your objects can't be read for hours, yet not one byte is lost. Which promise broke, and which held?
title: Durable, available, reliable: three different promises
body:
Teams say "the data must be safe" and mean different things. **Durability** means the data still exists and is correct, even if you cannot reach it right now. **Availability** means you can read or write it right now. **Reliability** is the broad property of doing what the system promises over time, and includes both.

The first two can fail separately. In the 2017 Amazon S3 outage, objects in us-east-1 were unreadable for hours, yet no data was lost.
takeaway: A healthy dashboard can sit on top of wrong bytes.
deeper:
**Durable, not available:** S3 in February 2017 is the classic case. The index and placement subsystems needed full restarts, reads failed for hours, and the data was all still there once they finished.

**Available, not durable:** The opposite is sneakier. A system can answer every request quickly while returning silently corrupted bytes. Error rates are flat, latency is low, health checks pass. That is a durability failure hiding behind a healthy dashboard, and availability monitoring cannot see it. Only integrity checks, such as end-to-end checksums, catch it.

**Ask for both:** The two goals have different costs and different designs. When a product owner says the data must be safe, ask which they mean: never lost, always reachable, or both. That answer decides whether you spend on redundancy and repair, on failover capacity, or on both.

quiz.q: Your storage cluster reports 100% availability and 5 ms p99 latency all month. A customer says downloaded files won't open. What kind of failure is this, and why didn't monitoring catch it?
quiz.a: A durability failure: the data is reachable but wrong. Availability metrics (errors, latency) only measure reachability, so they stay green. Only integrity checks such as end-to-end checksums detect wrong bytes.

mcq.q: During the 2017 S3 us-east-1 outage, objects were unreadable for hours. What was lost?
options: Availability only; no data was lost
Durability only; reads kept working
Both availability and some data
Neither; only writes were delayed
mcq.why: Objects could not be read, an availability failure, but every byte survived. Durable-but-unavailable is exactly this case.

hook: A datasheet promises 1 million hours before a drive fails. What share of your fleet dies each year?
title: An MTTF of 1 million hours still kills 0.88% a year
body:
Vendors quote **MTTF**, mean time to failure, often 1 to 2.5 million hours. That sounds like drives last forever. It says nothing of the sort, because MTTF describes a fleet, not one drive.

Convert it to the number planners use, the **annualized failure rate (AFR)**: the fraction of drives that fail in a year. AFR is roughly 8,760 hours (one year) divided by MTTF. So 1 million hours means an AFR of about 0.88%, which tells you how many drives you will replace.
takeaway: Divide 8,760 by the MTTF before you believe a datasheet.
deeper:
**The conversion:** A year has 8,760 hours. With an MTTF of 1 million hours, about 8,760 / 1,000,000, or 0.88%, of a large fleet fails each year. At 2.5 million hours the datasheet implies about 0.35%.

**The catch:** Those figures come from vendor lab tests. Real fleets are messier. Some models are much worse than average, and failure rates vary with drive age. The best public data comes from Backblaze, a cloud backup and storage company that has published statistics on its own fleet every quarter since 2013. Real fleets see AFR around 1 to 2% per year.

**Why it matters:** AFR sets your repair load, your spare capacity, and the λ in every durability calculation. Plan from the datasheet and you underestimate all three. Convert any quoted MTTF and compare it with fleet data before trusting it.

quiz.q: A vendor pitches drives with a 2.5 million hour MTTF, so your team budgets for 0.35% annual failures. What should you check before approving the spare-parts budget?
quiz.a: Real fleet data. Vendor MTTF comes from lab tests; fleets like Backblaze's see roughly 1 to 2% AFR, varying by model and age. Budget from fleet numbers, not the datasheet.

mcq.q: Roughly what AFR does an MTTF of 1 million hours imply?
options: About 0.88% per year
About 8.8% per year
About 0.088% per year
About 1 failure per million drives
mcq.why: AFR is roughly 8,760 hours divided by MTTF: 8,760 / 1,000,000 ≈ 0.88%.

hook: One company has published failure stats for its own drives every quarter since 2013. What do they show?
title: 344,196 drives, 1.36% dead in a year
body:
Vendor datasheets come from lab tests. Backblaze, a cloud backup and storage company, publishes failure statistics from its own fleet every quarter, and has since 2013.

For 2025 it reported an overall AFR of 1.36% across 344,196 hard drives and 30 models. It was 1.55% for 2024 (recomputed) and 1.70% for 2023. Some individual models were much worse than average, and rates vary with drive age. Plan for **bad batches**.
takeaway: Plan with fleet numbers, and assume one drive model is a lemon.
deeper:
**Why it's the reference:** It is the best public data on how drives behave in a real fleet rather than a lab. The 2025 average, λ = 0.0136 per year, is a sensible input to a back-of-envelope durability calculation.

**The average hides risk:** A fleet AFR of 1.36% can contain a model failing much more often. Drives from the same manufacturing batch fail together, so if all three replicas of an object sit on one flawed batch, their failures are not independent, and durability math that multiplies small probabilities stops holding. Spreading copies across failure domains, and ideally across drive models, limits this.

**Age drifts too:** Failure rates change as drives get older, so a fleet's AFR moves over time. The repair system has to absorb shifting failure counts without help.

**The rule of thumb:** Real drives fail at around 1 to 2% per year, so at scale several die every day.

quiz.q: Your fleet-wide AFR matches Backblaze's 1.36%, yet all three replicas of one object failed within a week. What likely went wrong in placement?
quiz.a: The replicas probably sat on drives from the same model or batch. Same-batch drives fail together, so the failures were correlated, not independent. Spread replicas across failure domains and drive models.

mcq.q: Backblaze reported a 2025 fleet AFR of 1.36%. What is the main caution in using that number?
options: Some models fail much more often than average
It counts only drives younger than one year
It comes from vendor lab tests, not a fleet
It covers solid-state drives, not hard drives
mcq.why: The average hides variation: some models were much worse and rates change with age, so expect bad batches.

predict.q: Backblaze tracked 344,196 hard drives through 2025. What share of them failed during the year?
options: About 1.4%
About 0.1%
About 5%

hook: Your fleet has 100,000 good drives. How often should someone get paged for a dead disk?
title: 100,000 drives means about 4 dead ones every day
body:
Multiply fleet size by AFR. At about 1.4%, 100,000 drives lose about 1,400 a year, roughly 4 every day, weekends included. Companies with millions of drives see far more.

At that scale a drive failure is not an incident. It is a constant background process, like garbage collection. The system must detect each failure and re-create the lost copies automatically, with no human in the loop.
takeaway: If a dead disk pages a human, your design won't survive growth.
deeper:
**The arithmetic:** Failures per year equal fleet size times AFR. 100,000 × 0.014 = 1,400. Divide by 365 and you get about 4 a day. Grow the fleet tenfold and it is about 40 a day, every day.

**Repair is a subsystem:** Healing needs its own budget. It needs spare disk space to rebuild into, network bandwidth reserved so repair and user traffic do not starve each other, and automation that chooses where new copies go while keeping them in separate failure domains.

**Speed is durability:** Data is at risk only while a copy is missing. A manual process that takes a day to notice and replace a drive leaves that drive's data exposed for a day, and it happens four times a day across the fleet. Fast automatic healing is both an operational necessity and the main lever on durability.

quiz.q: Your team runs 1 million drives at 1.4% AFR and handles each failure with a ticket and a runbook. Estimate the daily ticket count and say why it is also a durability problem.
quiz.a: About 38 a day (14,000 a year). Manual handling stretches each repair window, and data stays exposed until a new copy exists, so slow humans directly lower durability.

mcq.q: At 1.4% AFR, about how many drives fail per day in a 100,000-drive fleet?
options: About 4
About 40
About 1,400
About 1 per week
mcq.why: 100,000 × 1.4% = 1,400 per year; divided by 365 days, that is roughly 4 per day.

hook: Two clusters have identical drives and identical failure rates. One is hundreds of times safer. How?
title: You only lose data when failures overlap
body:
Three replicas on three drives means one dead drive loses nothing. You lose data only if all three fail before you finish making a new copy. That time is the **repair time**, or **MTTR** (mean time to repair).

So your data is vulnerable only during the repair window. Make the window small, and overlapping failures become very rare. You cannot do much about how often drives fail. How fast you replace what was lost is yours to control.
takeaway: Durability is a race between the next failure and your repair.
deeper:
**It's a race:** When the first drive fails, a clock starts. If the second and third drives holding the same data fail before repair completes, the data is gone. If repair wins, you are back to three healthy copies and the race resets.

**Three levers:** Durability engineering obsesses over repair. Detection: how fast you notice the drive is dead. Prioritization: repair data that has lost the most copies first. Throughput: how fast the missing bytes can be rebuilt elsewhere.

**Why bigger drives hurt:** A larger drive holds more data, so rebuilding it from one source takes longer and the window stretches from hours to more than a day. Scatter data in small chunks across many drives, and repair runs in parallel and the window drops to minutes.

**The catch:** This assumes independent failures. A power event or firmware bug can kill several copies at once and skip the race entirely.

quiz.q: Cluster A detects dead drives in 5 minutes and rebuilds in 1 hour. Cluster B has slightly better drives but takes 2 days to swap them by hand. Which is likely more durable, and why?
quiz.a: A. Loss needs further failures to land inside the repair window, and A's window is over 40 times shorter. Window length outweighs a modest difference in drive failure rate.

mcq.q: With three replicas, when can data actually be lost?
options: When all three copies fail within one repair window
Whenever any single drive holding a copy fails
When two drives fail anywhere in the same year
Only when a whole data center loses power
mcq.why: One failure opens a repair window; loss needs the other two copies to fail before the rebuild finishes.

hook: Three replicas, 1.36% yearly drive failures, one-day repair. What are the odds you lose an object this year?
title: One-day repair, three copies: about 10 nines
body:
Label the assumptions: three replicas on independent drives, AFR λ = 0.0136 per year, repair time T. Loss needs a chain. One of 3 drives fails (rate 3λ per year). Before repair, one of the other 2 fails (about 2λT). Then the last one fails (about λT).

Multiply: yearly loss probability per object is about 6 × λ³ × T². With T = 1 day, that is about 1.1 × 10^-10, roughly 10 nines.
takeaway: You can't change λ much. T is yours to shrink.
deeper:
**Plugging in:** With T = 1 day (1/365 year), λT is 3.7 × 10^-5 and yearly loss probability is about 1.1 × 10^-10. With T = 1 hour (1/8,760 year), λT is 1.6 × 10^-6 and loss is about 2 × 10^-13, roughly 12 to 13 nines.

**Why T is squared:** After the first failure, two more drives must each fail inside the window. Each chance is proportional to T, so together they scale with T². That squared term is where faster repair pays off.

**The catch:** Independence is a big and unrealistic assumption. Same-batch drives, a power event, a firmware bug or a bad deploy take out several copies together, so real risk is higher than this model says.

**What to keep:** Not the exact number, the shape. Loss grows with the cube of the failure rate and the square of repair time. Better drives nudge λ; software, placement and bandwidth shrink T.

quiz.q: One colleague halves λ by buying better drives. Another halves repair time. With three replicas, whose change cuts loss probability more on paper?
quiz.a: Halving λ cuts loss 8× (λ³); halving T cuts it 4× (T²). The drive upgrade wins on paper, but T is far cheaper to change through software and bandwidth.

mcq.q: In 6 × λ³ × T², where does the factor 6 come from?
options: 3 choices for the first failure × 2 for the second
Six failure domains in a typical region
The number of nines the model targets
A safety margin for correlated failures
mcq.why: The first failure has rate 3λ, the second probability 2λT, the third λT: 3 × 2 × 1 = 6.

predict.q: Three replicas, 1.36% yearly drive failure rate, one-day repair. What are the yearly odds of losing a given object?
options: About 1 in 10 billion
About 1 in 10,000
About 1 in a million

hook: Your repair jobs get 24× faster. Nothing else changes. How much safer is your data?
title: Repair 24× faster, lose data 576× less often
body:
Move repair time from 1 day to 1 hour, a 24× cut. With three replicas, loss probability scales with T², so risk drops about 576× (24 squared), from roughly 10 nines to 12 to 13.

The general rule: with n replicas, loss scales with T to the power (n − 1). After the first failure, n − 1 more failures must all land inside the repair window.

stat.label: lower loss risk from 24× faster repair

takeaway: With n replicas, loss scales with T^(n−1). Repair speed is durability.
deeper:
**Quick mental math:** Cut repair from 12 hours to 3 hours, a 4× reduction, and three-replica loss drops about 16×. With four replicas the exponent is 3, so the same 4× gives about 64×. With two replicas the exponent is 1, and you get only a proportional 4×.

**Why it's cheap:** Repair speed is mostly software and network bandwidth you already own: faster detection, repairing the most endangered data first, spreading data so many drives share the work. Extra hardware adds cost to every byte forever. A repair improvement protects all existing and future data once it is built.

**The catch:** The squared payoff assumes independent failures. It does nothing against a correlated event, such as a rack losing power, that wipes several copies in the same instant. Fast repair shrinks the window; only failure-domain placement stops copies dying together.

quiz.q: Your three-replica system repairs in 6 hours. Management wants 100× lower loss risk. Roughly what repair time gets you there, assuming independent failures?
quiz.a: About 36 minutes. Loss scales with T², so 100× needs a 10× shorter window: 6 hours divided by 10.

mcq.q: With four replicas, repair becomes 4× faster. Roughly how much does loss probability fall?
options: About 64×
About 16×
About 4×
About 256×
mcq.why: With n replicas, loss scales with T^(n−1). For n = 4, that is 4³ = 64.

predict.q: Repair time drops from 1 day to 1 hour, 24× faster. How much does three-replica loss risk fall?
options: About 576×
About 24×
About 48×

hook: A fourth replica makes the durability math much better. Storage engineers still usually say no. Why?
title: A 4th replica costs 33% more disk, forever
body:
A fourth replica genuinely improves the math: the exponent on repair time goes from 2 to 3. So why do storage engineers say faster repair matters more?

Cost first. A fourth replica adds 33% more disk for every byte you store, forever, and every new byte needs the extra copy too. Faster repair is mostly software and network bandwidth you already own. Cutting repair from 1 day to 1 hour already buys about 576× lower loss risk without one extra drive.
takeaway: Buy durability with software you own before disks you'll pay for forever.
deeper:
**The bill:** Going from three to four replicas multiplies raw storage by 4/3 across the whole fleet. At exabyte scale that is a vast purchase of disks, racks and power, and it never stops, because growth inherits it.

**The alternative:** Repair improvements are closer to one-time engineering. Detect failures faster. Repair data that has lost the most copies first. Scatter data so many drives share each rebuild. Reserve bandwidth for repair traffic. Once built, these protect every existing and future byte.

**Two more reasons:** Drives keep getting bigger, which makes whole-disk rebuilds dangerously slow, and parallel, declustered repair fixes that. Together they explain why GFS, Colossus, Tectonic and S3 chunk and scatter data rather than just adding copies.

**The catch:** None of this makes a fourth copy useless. It is the expensive knob, so turn the cheap one first.

quiz.q: You store 10 PB of logical data with three replicas, and repair takes a day. A proposal adds a fourth replica. What cheaper option should you evaluate first, and why?
quiz.a: Faster, parallel repair. A fourth replica adds another 10 PB of raw disk, 33% more, forever. Cutting repair to an hour gives about 576× lower risk using software and bandwidth you already own.

mcq.q: Why is a fourth replica usually a worse durability investment than faster repair?
options: It adds 33% more disk for every byte, forever
It lowers durability by adding a failure point
It cannot be placed in separate failure domains
It only helps when failures are correlated
mcq.why: Four copies instead of three means 33% more raw storage permanently, while faster repair mostly reuses software and bandwidth you own.

hook: Drives keep getting bigger. Why does that quietly make the data on them less safe?
title: A 24 TB rebuild from one disk: 33 hours exposed
body:
With whole-disk mirroring, a failed drive is rebuilt from one surviving disk, so that disk's bandwidth caps the repair. A 24 TB drive at 200 MB/s takes 24 × 10^12 / 2 × 10^8 = 120,000 seconds, about 33 hours.

For those 33 hours the data has one fewer copy. Bigger drives stretch the repair window unless you change the design.

stat.label: to rebuild 24 TB from one disk at 200 MB/s

takeaway: Bigger drives, same single source: the repair window grows with every generation.
deeper:
**Then vs now:** A 2 TB drive at the same 200 MB/s rebuilds in about 10,000 seconds, under 3 hours. A 24 TB drive takes over a day. That is a 12× longer window, and since three-replica loss scales with T², roughly 144× more loss risk for the same design.

**Worse in practice:** A rebuild competes with user traffic, so 200 MB/s may be optimistic on a busy day. The longer it runs, the more chance a correlated event, such as another drive from the same batch failing, lands inside it.

**The real fix:** Faster disks will not close the gap. Change placement so that many disks share the repair work, and the window shrinks from hours to minutes. That is declustered repair, and it is why large systems stopped mirroring whole disks. Whole-disk mirroring was fine at 2 TB. At 24 TB it is a day of exposure per failure.

quiz.q: Your cluster upgrades from 2 TB to 24 TB drives but keeps whole-disk mirroring at the same 200 MB/s. What happens to durability, and roughly by how much?
quiz.a: It drops. The rebuild window grows about 12× (under 3 hours to about 33), and three-replica loss scales with T², so risk rises roughly 144×.

mcq.q: What limits the rebuild speed of a whole-disk mirror?
options: The bandwidth of the one surviving source disk
The CPU cost of computing parity fragments
The number of racks in the failure domain
The metadata service's lookup rate
mcq.why: Mirroring copies the whole drive from one surviving disk, so repair time is capacity divided by that disk's throughput.

predict.q: A 24 TB drive dies. It is rebuilt from one mirror disk at 200 MB/s. How long is its data exposed?
options: About 33 hours
About 2 hours
About 12 minutes

hook: Same lost 24 TB drive. Each helper disk copies 10× slower than before, yet repair ends 100× sooner. How?
title: 1,000 drives rebuild 24 TB in about 20 minutes
body:
Spread a drive's data in small chunks across 1,000 other drives, and each survivor re-copies only a small piece. Even at 20 MB/s per drive, 1,000 drives rebuild 24 TB in about 1,200 seconds, roughly 20 minutes instead of 33 hours.

This is **declustered repair**. It is why GFS, Colossus, Tectonic and S3 split data into chunks and scatter them widely instead of mirroring whole disks.
takeaway: Don't make one disk fix a failure. Make a thousand disks each fix a sliver.
deeper:
**The numbers:** 1,000 drives × 20 MB/s is about 20 GB/s of aggregate repair bandwidth. Going from 33 hours to 20 minutes is about a 100× shorter window, which for three replicas means roughly 10,000× lower loss probability.

**Side by side:** Whole-disk mirror: one disk copies 24 TB, about 33 hours exposed. Scattered chunks: a thousand disks each copy a sliver, about 20 minutes exposed.

**Gentle on users:** 20 MB/s is a small slice of each drive's bandwidth, so user traffic barely notices. The new copies also land on many drives, avoiding a single hot spot.

**The catch:** Declustering costs metadata and placement complexity. The system must track where every chunk lives and keep the copies of each chunk in different failure domains. Any single drive failure now touches chunks of many objects, so repair must be fully automated.

quiz.q: Two designs lose the same 24 TB drive. A mirrors whole disks; B scatters small chunks across 1,000 drives. Why is B's data safer during the rebuild, even though each B drive copies slowly?
quiz.a: B rebuilds in parallel: 1,000 drives at 20 MB/s give about 20 GB/s, so the window is about 20 minutes versus 33 hours. Shorter windows make overlapping failures far rarer.

mcq.q: Why does declustered repair shrink the repair window?
options: Many drives each rebuild a small piece in parallel
Each drive copies data at a much higher speed
It skips copying data that is rarely read
It stores fewer copies, so less must be rebuilt
mcq.why: Aggregate bandwidth is the win: 1,000 drives at 20 MB/s rebuild 24 TB in about 20 minutes.

predict.q: A lost drive's 24 TB is scattered across 1,000 other drives, each copying at only 20 MB/s. How long does the rebuild take?
options: About 20 minutes
About 33 hours
About 3 hours

hook: A code that survives 4 lost pieces uses under half the disk of 3 full copies. What does it cost instead?
title: Erasure coding: 1.4× overhead, harder repairs
body:
Triple replication stores every byte 3 times. **Erasure coding** follows the same durability logic more cheaply. A 10+4 code splits data into 10 data fragments plus 4 parity fragments and survives any 4 lost, at 1.4× overhead.

The cost is repair. Rebuilding one lost fragment means reading from many other fragments, not copying one replica. Repair speed and repair traffic must be engineered carefully.

stat.label: storage overhead of a 10+4 code, vs 3×

takeaway: Erasure coding saves disk and spends network. Budget the repair traffic.
deeper:
**Durability math:** Losing data needs 5 of the 14 fragments to fail inside one repair window. If repair is fast and fragments live in independent failure domains, that is very rare.

**The saving:** 1.4× versus 3× means less than half the raw disk for the same logical data. At fleet scale that difference is enormous.

**The catch:** To rebuild one missing fragment, the system reads enough surviving fragments to reconstruct it. That is much more disk and network traffic per repaired byte than copying from a replica. Leave it unbudgeted and repair either runs slowly, stretching the exposure window, or floods the network and hurts user traffic.

**Same principles:** Scatter fragments widely, repair in parallel, and fix the stripes that have lost the most fragments first. The repair window still rules durability; erasure coding just makes it more expensive to keep short.

quiz.q: You move cold data from 3× replication to a 10+4 erasure code, and repair jobs start saturating the network. Why, and what should you tune?
quiz.a: Each rebuilt fragment requires reading many surviving fragments, so repair traffic multiplies. Throttle and spread repair, scatter fragments widely, and prioritize stripes with the most lost fragments.

mcq.q: A 10+4 erasure code can lose how many fragments and still recover the data?
options: Any 4 of its 14
Any 10 of its 14
Exactly 1, like a mirror
Any 4, but only data fragments
mcq.why: Any 10 surviving fragments can rebuild the data, so any 4 of the 14 can be lost.

hook: S3 says store 10 million objects and you'll lose one every 10,000 years. Who measured that?
title: S3's 11 nines is a model, not a measurement
body:
Amazon S3 says Standard storage is designed for 99.999999999% (**11 nines**) durability of objects over a year. The S3 FAQ puts it concretely: store 10,000,000 objects and on average you expect to lose one object every 10,000 years.

Nobody has run S3 for 10,000 years. The figure is a design target from a model, not a measured count. The model mostly covers hardware failure: independent-ish failures, repair times and placement across failure domains.
takeaway: Nines tell you what the model covers, not what can happen to you.
deeper:
**Where it comes from:** The same reasoning as a back-of-envelope durability calculation, applied with S3's real redundancy, repair speeds and placement. It describes how the system is engineered to survive hardware faults, not an audited loss history.

**What it's good for:** It tells you independent hardware failure is very well handled for this class of storage. That is real engineering and worth paying for.

**How it's misread:** People hear "my data cannot be lost." The model does not cover you deleting your own data, a bug in your application writing garbage, a compromised account, or a legal or billing event closing the account. Those are far more likely than an 11-nines event.

**What to do:** Treat the number as the floor the provider handles for you. Versioning, backups and separate accounts cover everything above it.

quiz.q: A startup advertises 12 nines of durability because it has run two years with zero lost objects. What's wrong with treating that as proof?
quiz.a: Nines are a model-based design target, not a measured count. Two loss-free years can't verify odds of one loss in thousands of years; inspect the model's assumptions instead.

mcq.q: What does S3's 11-nines durability figure represent?
options: A model-based design target for hardware failure
A measured loss rate from S3's operating history
A guarantee covering accidental customer deletes
An availability target for reads in one region
mcq.why: No one has run S3 for 10,000 years. The figure models hardware failure, repair and placement.

hook: Your bucket has 11 nines of durability. You run one wrong DELETE. How much do the nines help?
title: 11 nines won't save you from your own DELETE
body:
A common mistake is reading 11 nines as "my data cannot be lost." The model covers hardware. It does not cover you deleting your own data, a bug in your app writing garbage, a compromised account, or a legal or billing event closing the account.

To the storage system, none of these is a failure. Your delete is a successful request. Garbage is stored with perfect durability. Every redundant copy faithfully reflects the mistake, and these events are far more likely than 11-nines hardware losses.
takeaway: Storage keeps your mistakes with the same eleven nines as your data.
deeper:
**Outside the model:** Customer or operator deletes, application bugs, account compromise, provider control-plane mistakes and large correlated disasters all sit outside the hardware model. Together they cause almost all real losses.

**Why redundancy can't help:** An attacker with your credentials is an authorized user. A buggy writer is a valid client. None of these registers as a failure, so there is nothing for repair to fix.

**The provider version:** In May 2024, a parameter left blank a year earlier in a Google internal tool led to automatic deletion of UniSuper's whole private cloud, across two regions. Copies inside the provider did not help. Backups at a separate provider did.

**The right defenses:** Versioning, delayed or soft deletes, immutable backups, separate accounts and credentials, and at least one copy outside your primary provider's control plane.

quiz.q: A deploy ships a serializer bug that overwrites 2% of user profiles with empty records in an 11-nines object store. Why won't the store's durability help, and what would?
quiz.a: The store sees valid writes, not failures, so it durably keeps the empty records. Versioning, point-in-time backups or delayed deletes let you restore the old versions.

mcq.q: Which event is covered by S3's 11-nines durability model?
options: Independent drive failures inside S3
You deleting the wrong bucket
A bug in your app writing garbage
An account closed over billing
mcq.why: The model covers hardware failure with repair and placement. Deletes, bugs and account events are outside it.

hook: Durability math multiplies small odds into tiny ones. What real-world events make that multiplication wrong?
title: Correlated failures break the nines math
body:
Durability math multiplies probabilities, which works only if one failure tells you nothing about another. Real failures are **correlated**: one cause takes out many copies at once.

Drives from the same manufacturing batch fail together. A power event takes out a whole rack or building. A firmware bug hits every drive of a model. A software bug or bad deploy hits every server at once. Then several replicas die together, skipping the repair-window race entirely.
takeaway: Three copies that share a fate are one copy.
deeper:
**Why multiplication breaks:** If three replicas share a rack and the rack loses power, the chance they all die together is roughly the chance of the rack failing, not the cube of one drive's failure rate.

**Each cause, a response:** Batch effects: spread copies across drive models and purchase batches. Power and building events: spread across racks, power zones and buildings. Firmware bugs: roll firmware out gradually. Software bugs and bad deploys: deploy in stages, use cells, and keep backups the buggy software cannot touch.

**Software is the worst:** A bug in crash recovery, caching, compaction or garbage collection can lose or corrupt data across the whole fleet at once, breaking every independence assumption.

**The evidence:** Across six major public storage incidents, none was "too many disks failed at random." Each came from a cause that hit many machines at once or went around redundancy entirely.

quiz.q: Your three replicas sit on drives bought in one batch, installed in one rack. The nines calculation says 10 nines. Why is the real number much worse?
quiz.a: The copies share fates: same-batch drives fail together, and one rack power event kills all three. Failures are correlated, so multiplying independent probabilities overstates durability.

mcq.q: Which of these is a correlated failure?
options: A firmware bug hitting every drive of one model
One drive wearing out after five years
A single sector going bad on one disk
One server's fan failing in a large fleet
mcq.why: Correlated failures share a cause. A firmware bug strikes every drive of that model at once, defeating replica independence.

hook: Four lightning strikes hit a Google zone's power grid. Why wouldn't extra replicas in that zone have helped?
title: Four lightning strikes, one correlated failure
body:
In August 2015, four lightning strikes on the local power grid hit Google's europe-west1-b zone. Google reported that less than 0.000001% of Persistent Disk space in the zone was permanently lost, and about 5% of Standard Persistent Disks saw at least one I/O failure.

The loss was tiny, but it came from one correlated event, not independent drive failures. Every copy in the zone shared the same power. Google's fixes included hardware that keeps cached data safe across power loss.
takeaway: More copies behind the same power feed add cost, not safety.
deeper:
**What changed:** Nothing about individual drive reliability. One external event hit many machines in the same instant, so any protection that depended on copies inside that zone was exposed at once.

**The amplifier:** Volatile cache during power loss. Data held in a cache that loses its contents when power drops is exposed, no matter how many disks sit behind it.

**The fix:** A persistent write path: hardware that keeps cached data safe across power loss. That targets the correlated weakness directly. More replicas in the same zone would all have shared the same power event.

**The general rule:** Durability needs copies that do not share a fate. That is the idea behind failure domains: placing replicas across disks, hosts, racks, power zones and buildings. A zone is one failure domain, however many disks it holds.

quiz.q: After a zone-wide power event, a teammate proposes adding a fourth replica in the same zone. Why is that the wrong fix, and what addresses the actual failure?
quiz.a: All in-zone copies share the same power, so they fail together. Fix the correlated weakness: a persistent write path so cached data survives power loss, plus copies in other failure domains.

mcq.q: What turned Google's 2015 lightning strikes into permanent data loss?
options: Volatile cache during power loss
Too many drives failing at random
An operator deleting the wrong disk
A bad software deploy to storage nodes
mcq.why: Cached data was exposed when power failed; the design fix was a persistent write path that survives power loss.

hook: Three replicas on three disks. One event destroys all three. What did the placement get wrong?
title: Three copies only count if they don't share a fate
body:
Three replicas on three disks in one host are one host failure away from loss. Real systems place replicas or erasure-coded fragments across **failure domains**: sets of components that can fail together from one cause. Think disks, hosts, racks, power zones and often buildings (availability zones).

The durability math only holds if the copies do not share a fate. Three copies in three buildings survive a whole building going dark.
takeaway: Count failure domains, not copies.
deeper:
**A hierarchy:** A disk can fail alone. A host failure takes its disks. A rack failure, through its switch or power, takes its hosts. A power zone takes many racks. A building takes everything inside it. Placement policy decides at which level copies must be separated.

**Wider costs more:** Cross-building placement means writes travel farther and repair traffic crosses pricier links. Systems choose the separation level from how critical the data is and how much write latency they can tolerate.

**Not just hardware:** A shared control plane, account or contract is also a failure domain. UniSuper's data sat in two Google Cloud regions, and one provider-side deletion removed both. A bug deployed everywhere at once is a failure domain spanning the whole fleet, which is why staged rollouts and cells matter.

quiz.q: Your team spreads replicas across three regions of one cloud account, all managed by one automation pipeline. Which failure domain do all three still share?
quiz.a: The account and control plane. One bad automation run, compromised credential or provider-side deletion can hit every region at once, as UniSuper's two-region deletion showed.

mcq.q: Why are replicas spread across racks and buildings rather than disks in one host?
options: So no single cause can destroy every copy
So each write completes faster
So repair traffic stays cheaper
So each copy can serve different users
mcq.why: Durability math assumes copies fail independently. Separate failure domains ensure one event, like a host or power loss, cannot hit all copies.

hook: Someone shows you a slide claiming 12 nines of durability. Which of your questions matters most?
title: Three questions to ask about any 'N nines' claim
body:
When someone shows you "N nines," ask three questions. What failure model: independent or correlated? What repair time is assumed, and is it measured at p99 during a busy day? What is outside the model: operator error, software bugs, deletes?

The honest answer to the third usually matters more than the number. That is where real data loss comes from, and no nines calculation includes it.
takeaway: The most important line of any durability model is what it leaves out.
deeper:
**The failure model:** Independence is the big assumption. A number computed with independent failures can overstate durability by orders of magnitude if copies share batches, racks or software.

**The repair time:** Three-replica loss scales with T². A design that quotes 1-hour repair but takes 10 hours at p99 when the network is busy is about 100× less durable than claimed. Measure the busy day, not the quiet median.

**Out of the model:** Operator error, tooling and configuration mistakes, and deletes triggered most major public incidents: the S3 2017 typo, the GitLab wrong-server delete, the Azure 2014 config error, the UniSuper blank parameter. The rest, a DynamoDB network blip and lightning at Google, were correlated events. None appears in a nines calculation.

**The shift:** From "how many nines?" to "what are we not protected against?"

quiz.q: A design doc claims 12 nines assuming 1-hour repair. You learn repair actually takes 4 hours at p99 on busy days. Roughly how much did the doc overstate durability, for three replicas?
quiz.a: About 16×. Loss scales with T², and the real window is 4× longer. That is more than a whole nine gone, before counting correlated failures or deletes.

mcq.q: Which question about an 'N nines' claim usually matters most?
options: What failures are outside the model
How many replicas the design stores
Which vendor supplied the drives
What the median repair time is
mcq.why: Operator error, software bugs and deletes cause most real loss and never appear in the nines.

section: 10.3 Data corruption: when bytes change silently
hook: A byte changes on disk and nothing reports an error. What happens next, if nobody checks?
title: Silent corruption gets copied, backed up and served
body:
Losing a drive is loud: the system notices and repairs it. **Silent data corruption** is worse. Bytes change and nothing reports an error. Reads succeed, dashboards stay green, and the data is simply wrong.

If you do not detect it, your own protections spread it. You replicate the bad bytes, back them up, and serve them to users, each mechanism faithfully copying whatever it is given.
takeaway: Undetected corruption turns your safety nets into delivery systems.
deeper:
**Loud vs silent:** A dead drive triggers automatic repair. A flipped bit in a stored block triggers nothing until something reads that block and checks it, which for cold data may be years later.

**The spread:** Meanwhile, everything downstream treats the bad data as valid. Replication copies it to other nodes. Backups capture it, and older good backups may age out of retention. Migrations move it to new hardware. Caches serve it. By the time anyone notices, every copy may be bad.

**Two kinds of protection:** Replicas protect against loss, a copy disappearing. Checksums and scrubbing protect against wrong bytes, a copy that exists but is incorrect. You need both.

**The sources:** Aging media, misdirected or lost writes, firmware bugs, memory bit flips, network errors that slip past TCP checksums, your own software, and even CPUs that compute wrong answers.

quiz.q: A block in a cold photo archive silently flipped two years ago. Nightly backups ran the whole time, kept for 30 days. Why might none of your backups help?
quiz.a: Every backup since the flip captured the corrupt bytes, and good backups older than 30 days have aged out. Without detection, backups preserve the corruption.

mcq.q: Why is silent corruption more dangerous than a dead drive?
options: Nothing raises an error, so bad bytes spread
It only strikes data that is read often
Replication refuses to copy corrupted blocks
It can only be fixed by replacing hardware
mcq.why: No error means no repair; replication, backups and caches copy the wrong bytes until every copy may be bad.

section: 10.3 Data corruption: when bytes change silently
hook: TCP checks every packet you send. Why do storage systems still refuse to trust it?
title: Corruption hides in disks, wires, code and CPUs
body: Every layer checks its own hop, and every layer misses something. **Bit rot**: magnetic and flash cells degrade, and the drive's error-correcting code (ECC) catches most errors but not all. Misdirected or lost writes, firmware bugs and memory bit flips. Network corruption: TCP checksums are only 16 bits, so rare corruptions slip through at scale. Software bugs in your own code. And CPUs that compute wrong answers.
takeaway: Each layer checks its own hop. Only the ends can check the journey.
deeper:
**Rare times huge:** Drive ECC catches the vast majority of media errors, yet at fleet scale the rare misses still happen regularly.

**The nastiest disk error:** A misdirected write reports success, leaves stale data where it was meant to go, and overwrites some other location. Two blocks are now wrong and no error was raised.

**Why 16 bits is not enough:** A 16-bit checksum misses roughly one in 65,536 random corruptions. At the traffic volume of a large storage system, corrupted packets that happen to pass TCP's check will occur. TCP is not an integrity guarantee.

**Code and silicon:** Software bugs are the broadest source: serialization errors, wrong offsets, races in caching or compaction. The most surprising source is defective CPUs that silently compute wrong results.

**The fix:** Check integrity end to end, from the client that created the data to the reader.

quiz.q: Your storage service relies on TCP checksums in transit and drive ECC at rest, with no checksums of its own. At petabytes a day, why will corrupted data still reach users?
quiz.a: TCP's 16-bit checksum and drive ECC each miss a small fraction of errors, and neither covers memory flips, misdirected writes, software bugs or bad CPUs. At scale, small fractions become real corruption.

mcq.q: Why can't TCP checksums guarantee data integrity for a large storage system?
options: They are only 16 bits, so rare errors pass at scale
They are computed only when a connection opens
They cover packet headers but never the payload
They are disabled inside most data centers
mcq.why: A 16-bit checksum misses a small fraction of random corruptions; at storage traffic volumes that fraction becomes real corrupted data.

section: 10.3 Data corruption: when bytes change silently
hook: Your storage server checksums every block it receives. Why might that protect nothing at all?
title: Checksum early, verify late
body:
Per-layer checks leave gaps between layers. The **end-to-end argument** says check integrity at the ends. A checksum, such as CRC32C or SHA-256, is a small fingerprint of the data.

The client computes it when the data is created. Every layer stores and forwards it. Every read, copy, repair and migration verifies it. On a mismatch, the system reads another replica and repairs the bad one.
takeaway: A checksum taken after the damage just certifies the damage.
deeper:
**Why early matters:** A checksum computed by the storage server after the data crossed a buggy network card protects nothing. It fingerprints bytes that are already corrupted, and every later check passes. Computed by the client, it covers every hop in between: network, proxy, server, disk, repair and migration.

**Why late matters:** Verification must happen on every movement of data, not just user reads. Repair and migration are exactly when bad data could be copied onto fresh hardware and become the new source of truth.

**Choosing the fingerprint:** CRC32C is fast and has hardware support, which suits detecting accidental corruption at high throughput. Cryptographic hashes like SHA-256 are slower but also resist deliberate tampering.

**Self-healing:** With multiple replicas, a failed check stops being a disaster. Read a good copy, rewrite the bad one.

quiz.q: A proxy with a memory bug sits between clients and storage. The storage server computes a SHA-256 of what it receives. Will reads ever detect the proxy's corruption? How would you fix the design?
quiz.a: No: the server hashed already-corrupted bytes, so every check passes. Have the client compute the checksum before upload and verify it at every hop and on read.

mcq.q: Where should a checksum be computed for end-to-end protection?
options: By the client, when the data is created
By the storage server, on arrival
By the disk, when the block is written
By the backup system, each night
mcq.why: Computing it as early as possible covers every later hop; a server-side checksum can fingerprint already-corrupted bytes.

section: 10.3 Data corruption: when bytes change silently
hook: S3, GFS, HDFS, Ceph and ZFS differ in almost everything. Which integrity habit do they all share?
title: S3, GFS, HDFS, Ceph, ZFS: checksums everywhere
body:
Serious storage treats integrity as a baseline feature. Amazon S3 lets clients send checksums with uploads (CRC32, CRC32C, SHA-1, SHA-256, and later CRC64NVME). S3 verifies them and stores them with the object.

GFS stored a checksum for every 64 KB block of each chunk, and chunkservers verified data before returning it. HDFS, Ceph (with its BlueStore backend) and ZFS all store **per-block checksums**.
takeaway: Checksum at the size you read and repair, not the size you store.
deeper:
**S3 is end to end:** The client computes the checksum before upload, S3 verifies it on arrival, which catches corruption in transit, and stores it with the object. The algorithm list lets clients trade speed (CRC variants) against stronger cryptographic hashes (SHA variants).

**Why 64 KB blocks:** GFS chunks were large. One checksum per chunk would mean rereading the whole chunk to verify any part of it, and one bad bit would condemn the entire chunk. Per-block checksums let a chunkserver verify only the blocks being read and repair only the damaged block from another replica.

**Verify before serving:** Checking before returning data stops a corrupt block from reaching a client or being copied to another chunkserver during re-replication.

**Every layer:** HDFS, Ceph BlueStore and ZFS show the same pattern across distributed file systems, object stores and local file systems.

quiz.q: You design a blob store with 1 GB objects and one checksum per object. A user reads 4 KB, and one bit in the object is bad. What two problems does coarse checksumming cause?
quiz.a: Verifying the 4 KB read means rereading the whole 1 GB object, and the bad bit condemns the whole object instead of one small block. Per-block checksums fix both.

mcq.q: What did GFS chunkservers do with their per-64 KB checksums?
options: Verified data before returning it
Sent them to the master for storage
Computed them only in nightly scrubs
Used them to pick the primary replica
mcq.why: Chunkservers checked each block before serving it, so corrupt data never reached clients or re-replication.

section: 10.3 Data corruption: when bytes change silently
hook: Checksums catch corruption the moment data is read. What about a photo nobody opens for five years?
title: Scrubbing: read everything before it rots
body:
Checksums only help when someone reads the data. Cold data, like old photos and old logs, may sit unread for years. By then, two of three replicas might be silently bad.

**Scrubbing** is a background process that reads all data on a schedule, verifies checksums and repairs bad copies from good ones. The cost is I/O that competes with real traffic, so most systems throttle scrubbers and cover all data every few weeks.
takeaway: Find the first bad copy while good ones still exist.
deeper:
**Proactive detection:** Without scrubbing, corruption in cold data accumulates. Each replica decays on its own, and if nobody looks, eventually every copy of some object may be damaged and repair becomes impossible. Scrubbing catches the first bad copy while good ones remain and fixes it, resetting the clock.

**The schedule trade-off:** Scrubbing means reading the entire dataset, an enormous amount of disk I/O at scale. Run it too aggressively and user requests slow down. Run it too rarely and more corruption piles up between passes. Every few weeks, throttled when user traffic is high, is the common compromise.

**Two nets:** Read-path verification catches corruption in hot data quickly. Scrubbing makes sure cold data is checked too. For a 1-billion-user app, photos nobody has viewed in years are exactly what scrubbing exists to protect.

quiz.q: Your team disables the scrubber to cut disk load, since every read already verifies checksums. Which data is now at risk, and how does the risk grow?
quiz.a: Cold data nobody reads. Corruption accumulates unseen, and eventually all replicas of some objects may go bad, leaving no good copy to repair from.

mcq.q: What is scrubbing's main cost?
options: Disk I/O that competes with user traffic
Extra replicas stored for every object
Downtime while each disk is scanned
Rewriting every block on each pass
mcq.why: Scrubbing reads all data, so it is throttled and spread over weeks to avoid slowing real requests.

section: 10.3 Data corruption: when bytes change silently
hook: You add a fourth replica to protect against bit rot. How much safer is your data from corruption?
title: More replicas don't catch a single bad byte
body:
A common mistake is treating replication as protection against corruption. If corruption is not detected, the replication system copies the bad data faithfully to every replica.

The two mechanisms solve different problems. Replicas protect against **loss**: a copy disappearing because a drive, host or rack died. Checksums and scrubbing protect against **wrong bytes**: a copy that still exists but is incorrect. Without integrity checks, the system cannot even tell which copy is right.
takeaway: Replicas protect against loss. Checksums protect against lies.
deeper:
**Why the confusion:** Replication feels like safety, and it is, for the failure it targets. When a drive dies, a replica serves the data. Corruption is different: nothing is missing, a copy is present and simply wrong.

**Replication can spread it:** If the primary's copy is corrupted before or during a write, the corrupt bytes are replicated. If repair rebuilds a lost copy from a silently corrupted replica, the new copy is corrupt too. Without verification during repair, a system can replace good data with bad.

**With checksums, it flips:** A failed check identifies the bad copy, and the good replicas become the repair source. Replication plus integrity checks is the working combination.

**The bigger sibling:** Treating replication as a backup. Replication copies deletes and bad writes just as faithfully as it copies corrupted bytes.

quiz.q: Replica 3 disagrees with replicas 1 and 2, and your system has no checksums. Majority vote picks the version on 1 and 2. Why might that still be wrong?
quiz.a: If the corruption happened before replication, both matching replicas hold the same bad bytes. Without a checksum from the source, agreement proves consistency, not correctness.

mcq.q: What protects stored data against silent corruption?
options: Checksums plus scrubbing
Adding more replicas
Synchronous replication
Spreading copies across zones
mcq.why: Replicas guard against loss; only integrity checks detect wrong bytes and identify which copy is good.

section: 10.3 Data corruption: when bytes change silently
hook: For decades engineers assumed a broken CPU fails loudly. What did Meta find in hundreds of its CPUs?
title: Meta found hundreds of CPUs silently computing wrong
body:
Engineers long assumed that if a CPU makes a mistake, it crashes or reports a machine-check error. In 2021, Meta's paper Silent Data Corruptions at Scale (Dixit et al.) showed that assumption fails at scale.

Monitoring hundreds of thousands of machines for more than 18 months, Meta found hundreds of CPUs with manufacturing defects that produce wrong results with no error signal. In one case, a CPU computed a math function wrongly, and files went missing from a compressed database.
takeaway: Trusting a single computation is a bet you lose at fleet scale.
deeper:
**From math error to lost files:** A wrong result from one math function, used while processing a compressed database, meant files went missing. No crash, no error log, nothing flagged. The database was simply incomplete.

**Why checksums can miss it:** The error happens in computation, not storage. If the CPU computes data wrongly before a checksum is taken, the checksum faithfully protects the wrong data.

**Rare per machine, certain per fleet:** Hundreds of defective CPUs among hundreds of thousands of machines is a small rate, but a large fleet will always contain some.

**Meta's conclusion:** Fixing this needs three things together: hardware resilience, production detection, and fault-tolerant software that does not blindly trust a single computation. Google's HotOS paper the same year, Cores that don't count, found the same class of silently faulty CPUs.

quiz.q: Your storage node compresses a block, then checksums the compressed output. A defective core miscomputes during compression. Will any later read detect the problem?
quiz.a: Not via the checksum: it was computed over already-wrong output, so it matches. Only decompressing and comparing against the original, ideally on another machine, reveals the error.

mcq.q: What did Meta conclude was needed against silent CPU data corruption?
options: Hardware resilience, production detection, fault-tolerant software
Replacing every CPU older than 18 months
Adding ECC memory to every server
Running each job twice on the same core
mcq.why: No single layer suffices; Meta called for better hardware, detection in production, and software that doesn't trust one computation.

section: 10.3 Data corruption: when bytes change silently
hook: A CPU core encrypts your data, decrypts it to double-check, gets a perfect match. The data is already ruined.
title: The CPU bug that passed its own test
body:
Engineers assumed a faulty CPU crashes or throws an error. Google's HotOS 2021 paper, Cores that don't count, found **mercurial cores**: cores that silently compute wrong answers, a few per several thousand machines.

The eeriest case was a deterministic AES mis-computation that was self-inverting. The core made the same mistake encrypting and decrypting, so its own check passed. Only when a different core tried to decrypt did the stored data fail.
takeaway: Never let a machine grade its own work before an irreversible step.
deeper:
**Why the check was meaningless:** Encrypt, then decrypt and compare, is the standard sanity check. On the faulty core it passed perfectly, because the core made the same error in both directions. The ciphertext written to storage was wrong in a way only a correct core would notice. If the plaintext was deleted after that local check, the data was gone. You were grading the student with the student's own answer key.

**Keys raise the stakes:** The paper notes that a corrupted encryption key can make large amounts of data permanently unreadable. One faulty computation can lose everything that key protects.

**How often:** On the order of a few mercurial cores per several thousand machines, so a large fleet always has some. Defects can appear with age and temperature, so a core that passed once can go bad later.

**The defense:** Verify on a different machine before any irreversible step.

quiz.q: Your pipeline encrypts a file, decrypts it on the same core to verify, then deletes the plaintext. Why is that unsafe against a mercurial core, and what is the fix?
quiz.a: A self-inverting fault makes the same error both ways, so the local check passes on bad ciphertext. Decrypt on a different machine before deleting the plaintext.

mcq.q: Why did Google's self-inverting AES bug pass its own check?
options: The same core made the same error encrypting and decrypting
The checksum was computed before encryption
The key was cached in a different core
The bug only appeared under high temperature
mcq.why: Encrypt and decrypt on the one faulty core cancel out, so a same-core check can't see the corrupted ciphertext.

section: 10.3 Data corruption: when bytes change silently
hook: A faulty CPU core in a storage server can do more damage than a faulty disk. What does it touch?
title: Bad cores forge checksums and corrupt indexes
body:
A storage server's CPU computes checksums, compression, encryption and erasure codes. A bad core can produce a valid-looking checksum over wrong data, or corrupt an index that points to millions of objects.

Fleets fight back three ways. Screen the fleet repeatedly, because defects appear with age and temperature. Verify on a different machine, for example decrypting on another core before deleting the plaintext. **Quarantine** suspect cores so they stop touching data.
takeaway: Test CPUs like disks: repeatedly, forever, assuming some are already bad.
deeper:
**Every computation is an entry point:** Compression: output that decompresses to wrong data. Encryption: ciphertext only the faulty core can read. Erasure coding: parity that reconstructs garbage when a repair finally needs it. Checksums: a matching fingerprint over incorrect bytes.

**Screen repeatedly:** A CPU can pass acceptance testing and develop faults later as it ages or runs hot. Continuous production testing, running known computations and comparing with known answers, finds cores that have drifted.

**Verify elsewhere:** Cross-machine verification is the direct fix for self-inverting bugs. Before deleting plaintext, decrypt on another machine. The extra compute is spent only where a mistake would be irreversible.

**Quarantine:** Once a core is suspected, pull it from service rather than letting it keep producing subtly wrong results. A disk that dies stops doing harm; a core that lies keeps working.

quiz.q: A core passed burn-in when its server was installed three years ago. Why isn't that enough to trust it with erasure-coding computations today?
quiz.a: Defects appear with age and temperature, so a core that passed once can go bad later. Fleets must re-screen repeatedly and quarantine suspect cores.

mcq.q: Why must fleets screen CPUs repeatedly, not just at purchase?
options: Defects can appear with age and temperature
Firmware updates reset earlier test results
Burn-in tests cannot detect wrong answers
Screening is only accurate under full load
mcq.why: A core can pass acceptance testing and later start computing wrong results as it ages or runs hot.

section: 10.3 Data corruption: when bytes change silently
hook: One corrupted photo ruins one user's day. Which few bytes could ruin a million users' photos at once?
title: Guard metadata and keys harder than photos
body:
For a 1-billion-user app, the most dangerous place for silent corruption is not a single photo. It is **metadata and keys**: the index that maps photo IDs to locations, or the key that encrypts a million photos.

A corrupted photo affects one object. A corrupted index entry or key can make millions of objects unreachable or unreadable. Protect them with extra checks, multiple independent computations, and backups verified on different hardware.
takeaway: Protect bytes in proportion to how many other bytes they point to.
deeper:
**Leverage per byte:** Most bytes are payload, and corrupting one affects one object. A few bytes, such as index entries, placement maps and encryption keys, decide whether huge amounts of payload can be found or decrypted at all.

**A worked case:** A metadata server with a mercurial core that miscomputes CRC32C could produce checksums that match corrupted data, or corrupt an index affecting many objects. Defenses: client-computed end-to-end checksums verified on a different machine, repeated fleet screening and quarantine, and verified metadata backups.

**Cheap insurance:** Compute critical values twice on different machines and compare. Verify backups by restoring them on independent hardware. Metadata and keys are tiny next to the data they govern, so extra protection costs little.

**A recurring theme:** The S3 2017 and DynamoDB 2015 outages both centered on metadata subsystems.

quiz.q: You can afford to triple-verify one dataset: 2 PB of user photos or the 50 GB index mapping photo IDs to locations. Which do you pick, and why?
quiz.a: The index. A corrupted index entry can make millions of photos unreachable, while a corrupted photo affects one. It is also tiny, so extra checks and verified backups are cheap.

mcq.q: Why do metadata and encryption keys deserve extra protection?
options: One corrupt entry can affect millions of objects
They are read far more often than payload
They are stored on less reliable hardware
Checksums cannot be computed over them
mcq.why: An index entry or key governs many objects, so its corruption makes huge amounts of data unreachable or unreadable.

hook: Hardware fails at random, one machine at a time. What fails on every machine at once?
title: Software bugs, not hardware, are the biggest risk
body:
Hardware is not the biggest risk to stored data. Software bugs are. A storage node runs crash recovery, concurrency, caching, compaction and garbage collection. A bug in any of them can lose or corrupt data across the whole fleet at once, because every server runs the same code.

That breaks every independence assumption in durability math. And testing cannot cover every interleaving of concurrent operations and crashes, so large storage teams use **formal methods**: mathematically precise ways to specify and check behavior.
takeaway: A bug is a failure every replica shares.
deeper:
**Why software is different:** Hardware failures are mostly local, so redundancy absorbs them. A software bug is identical on every machine. Ship a flawed compaction routine and it can corrupt data on every node that compacts. Replicas do not help when all of them run the same code.

**Where bugs hide:** Crash recovery must rebuild correct state from whatever survived a power loss. Concurrency means operations interleave in countless orders. Caching creates copies of state that must agree. Compaction and garbage collection delete data in the background, so a mistake destroys data that looked unreferenced.

**Why tests struggle:** These bugs need rare combinations: two writes in one specific order, a crash at one exact instruction, a retry arriving mid-compaction. Tests sample a tiny fraction of possible orderings.

**The answer:** Define correct behavior precisely and let tools explore executions systematically. AWS uses TLA+ for designs and lightweight formal methods for ShardStore's code.

quiz.q: Your storage keeps five replicas across five zones. A new compaction release has a bug that drops live keys. How many replicas protect you, and why?
quiz.a: Effectively none. Every replica runs the same compaction code, so the bug hits all five, a perfectly correlated failure. Staged rollout, backups and formal checks are the defenses.

mcq.q: Why does a storage software bug defeat replication?
options: Every replica runs the same buggy code
Bugs only affect the primary replica
Replicas update too slowly to help
Bugs corrupt the network, not the disks
mcq.why: Identical code on every node means one bug fails all copies together, breaking the independence redundancy relies on.

hook: A DynamoDB bug hid behind a trace so long that no human reviewer was likely to spot it. What found it?
title: TLA+ found a DynamoDB bug 35 steps deep
body:
Some bugs appear only after a long, precise sequence of events. **TLA+** is a language for specifying a system's design: its states and allowed transitions. A model checker then explores all possible executions of a small version and reports violations.

AWS engineers wrote in Communications of the ACM (Newcombe et al., 2015) that they had used TLA+ since 2011 on systems including S3 and DynamoDB. It found subtle bugs that tests and reviews had missed.

stat.label: steps in a DynamoDB bug trace TLA+ found

takeaway: Tests sample the paths. Model checkers walk all of them, in miniature.
deeper:
**The standout bug:** One DynamoDB bug needed a sequence of 35 steps to appear. Humans are very unlikely to find a trace that long by reasoning or review, and random tests are unlikely to stumble into it. The model checker found it because it systematically explores every ordering in a small configuration.

**Why small works:** Real systems have thousands of nodes and unbounded data, which no tool can explore fully. But many design bugs appear with just a few nodes and a few operations. Checking every execution of a tiny system catches them before code is written.

**The catch:** TLA+ checks the design, not the code. Engineers can write code that diverges from a verified design, and the model checker will never know.

**Still worth it:** A flaw in a replication or recovery protocol found in a spec costs far less than one found after deployment across the fleet.

quiz.q: Your new replication protocol passed thousands of randomized tests and two design reviews. Why might a TLA+ model of a 3-node version still find a bug?
quiz.a: It explores every interleaving of the small model instead of sampling. Bugs needing long, precise sequences, like DynamoDB's 35-step trace, slip past random tests and human review.

mcq.q: What is the main limitation of TLA+ model checking?
options: It checks the design, not the actual code
It only works on systems with one node
It cannot find bugs involving concurrency
It requires a full mathematical proof
mcq.why: A verified spec says nothing about whether the implementation matches it.

predict.q: A model checker found a DynamoDB bug that appeared only after a specific sequence of steps. How long was it?
options: 35 steps
5 steps
3 steps

hook: AWS wanted formal checks on S3's real storage code, not just its design, without writing a full proof. How?
title: ShardStore: a hash map as the definition of correct
body:
TLA+ checks a design, but code can drift from it. For **ShardStore**, the key-value storage node inside Amazon S3, written in Rust, AWS checked the real code (Bornholt et al., SOSP 2021).

The team wrote **executable reference models**: simple versions of the system, such as a hash map, that define correct behavior. Property-based testing and model checking compared the implementation to the model, including under crashes and concurrency.

stat.label: issues kept out of production in ShardStore

takeaway: You don't need a proof. You need an executable definition of correct.
deeper:
**What it caught:** The approach prevented 16 issues from reaching production, including subtle crash-consistency and concurrency bugs, exactly the kind normal tests miss.

**How it works:**
1. Generate many random sequences of operations.
2. Apply each to both ShardStore and the simple model.
3. Inject crashes and explore concurrent interleavings.
4. Flag any result the model would not allow.
A hash map is easy to trust and a production storage node is not, so let the first judge the second.

**Why it stuck:** Normal engineers, not only formal-methods experts, extended the checks as the code changed. Because the reference models were simple and executable, verification kept pace with development instead of going stale.

**The lesson:** Skip the full proof. Write a precise, executable definition of "correct," and let automation check the real code against it every day.

quiz.q: Your team maintains a complex storage engine. One proposal is a full proof; another compares the engine to an in-memory map under random operations and injected crashes. Which did ShardStore choose, and why did it last?
quiz.a: The executable reference model. It checked real code, found crash and concurrency bugs, and stayed simple enough for ordinary engineers to extend as the code changed.

mcq.q: What served as ShardStore's definition of correct behavior?
options: A simple executable model, such as a hash map
A full machine-checked proof of the Rust code
A TLA+ specification of the whole S3 service
A suite of hand-written expected outputs
mcq.why: Reference models are simple implementations; the real code is automatically compared against them, including under crashes and concurrency.

predict.q: AWS checked ShardStore's real code against simple executable models. How many issues did that keep out of production?
options: Over 1,000

hook: At 10:00 someone deletes a table. You have three replicas and a 04:00 backup. Which still have the data?
title: Replication copies your mistakes. Backups undo them.
body:
**Replication** keeps copies in sync: when the primary changes, replicas follow within milliseconds or seconds. A **backup** is a copy from an earlier point in time, kept separately, that does not change when the primary does.

So replication protects against hardware failure. A bad delete at 10:00 reaches every replica within seconds. The 04:00 backup is still good: restore it, then replay logs up to 09:59.
takeaway: A backup's whole value is that it refuses to follow the primary.
deeper:
**Why it's structural:** Replication's job is to make copies identical as fast as possible. That is exactly what you want when a disk dies and exactly what you do not want when the change itself is the problem. Sync or async makes no difference: both deliver the delete, just milliseconds apart.

**What a backup needs:** Four properties, each blocking a failure:
1. Point-in-time, so you can go back before the mistake.
2. Immutable, so an attacker with admin rights cannot destroy it.
3. Independently stored, so an account or provider event cannot reach it.
4. Regularly restored, so you know it works.

**The single distinction:** Of everything in data protection, this matters most. Replicas survive broken hardware. Backups survive broken decisions.

quiz.q: Your database has synchronous replicas in three zones. At 14:00 an engineer runs a migration that drops a column. What can the replicas restore, and what do you actually need?
quiz.a: Nothing: they applied the drop within seconds. You need a backup from before 14:00, plus the log replayed to just before the migration.

mcq.q: Which failure does replication protect against?
options: A disk dying on the primary
A DELETE run on the wrong table
Ransomware encrypting the data
A bad schema migration
mcq.why: Replication copies every change almost instantly, so it saves you from hardware loss but spreads deletes, ransomware and bad migrations.

hook: A bug, a wrong rm -rf, ransomware, a bad migration. Why does your replication make each one worse?
title: Four disasters replication copies instantly
body:
Replication does not protect against four common disasters: a bug that writes bad data, a user or engineer running DELETE or rm -rf on the wrong thing, ransomware encrypting your data, and a bad schema migration.

In each case the primary receives a valid-looking change, and replication pushes it to every copy, often within seconds. Afterward all replicas are equally damaged, and no amount of redundancy brings back the old data.
takeaway: The system works perfectly. It is just doing the wrong thing.
deeper:
**Nothing failed:** From the storage system's view, a bug's writes are accepted writes. A delete is an authorized operation. Ransomware with stolen credentials looks like a normal client rewriting files. A migration is a deliberate change.

**The active-active trap:** Replicating to three regions in active-active mode multiplies the damage, not the protection. Every one of these four events lands in all three regions within seconds. You still need point-in-time backups, ideally immutable and in a separate account, and restores you have tested.

**The whitepaper agrees:** AWS's disaster recovery guidance says even active-active needs backups, because for corruption or deletion the recovery point is always before the disaster was discovered.

**In practice:** At GitLab in 2017, a delete hit the primary, and replication was useless because the secondary had just been wiped.

quiz.q: Ransomware with stolen admin credentials encrypts files on your primary. Your async replica lags by 30 seconds. Why does the lag not save you?
quiz.a: Within 30 seconds the encrypted writes replicate too; lag only delays the damage. You need a point-in-time, immutable backup the attacker cannot reach.

mcq.q: Why does replication spread a bad schema migration to every copy?
options: It is a valid change, so replicas apply it
Migrations bypass the replication log
Replicas lock the schema during writes
Only synchronous replication copies it
mcq.why: To storage, the migration is a legitimate write; replication's job is to apply every legitimate change everywhere.

hook: Snapshots are nearly instant and cost almost nothing to keep. Why aren't they backups?
title: A snapshot dies with the account that holds it
body:
A **snapshot** is a point-in-time image of a volume, file system or database. Most systems make them with **copy-on-write**: the snapshot shares blocks with live data, and only blocks that later change are copied. That makes snapshots fast and cheap.

The sharing is also the weakness. A snapshot in the same system and account dies with that system or account. Copy it somewhere else to make it a true backup.
takeaway: Cheap because it shares. Fragile for the same reason.
deeper:
**Why so fast:** Creating a snapshot just records which blocks exist at that moment. When live data changes a block, the old version is kept for the snapshot. Storage cost grows with the amount of change, not the size of the volume.

**Shared fate:** The snapshot and live data depend on the same storage, metadata and account. A bug that corrupts shared blocks hits both. A compromised, deleted or closed account takes the snapshots with it. If the provider deletes the whole environment, as happened to UniSuper in 2024, anything stored inside it, snapshots included, goes too.

**Right tool, right job:** Snapshots are great for fast recovery from small logical mistakes, like undoing a bad change from an hour ago. For disaster protection, copy them to another account, region or provider.

**Enable them first:** At GitLab in 2017, Azure disk snapshots were simply not enabled for the database servers.

quiz.q: Your team takes hourly snapshots of every production volume, stored in the production account. An attacker gains that account's admin credentials. What survives?
quiz.a: Probably nothing: the snapshots share the account, so the attacker can delete them along with the volumes. Copies in a separate account or provider would survive.

mcq.q: What turns a snapshot into a true backup?
options: Copying it outside the original system and account
Taking snapshots more frequently
Using copy-on-write for every block
Keeping it on the same volume as the data
mcq.why: In-place snapshots share storage and account with the live data, so they die with it. A copy elsewhere doesn't.

hook: A bad write lands at 10:00. Your last full backup is from 04:00. Must you lose six hours of work?
title: PITR: restore the backup, replay to 09:59
body:
Restore only the nightly backup and you lose every good write since. **Point-in-time recovery (PITR)** combines a full backup with a continuous log of changes, such as a write-ahead log or binlog. Restore the last full backup, then replay the log up to 09:59, just before the bad change.

Amazon RDS, Aurora, DynamoDB and Google Cloud SQL all offer PITR, typically with a retention window of days to weeks.
takeaway: PITR buys a tiny RPO and pays for it in replay time.
deeper:
**The gap it fills:** With nightly backups alone, a mistake at 10:00 means restoring 04:00 and losing six hours of good writes. With PITR the log fills in everything between the backup and the moment before the mistake.

**Best RPO for logical mistakes:** Bad writes, deletes and failed migrations are where PITR shines. RPO, the recovery point objective, is how much data you can afford to lose, and PITR gives the best RPO for these events.

**The catch:** Replay re-applies every change since the last full backup, in order. For a large, busy database that is a lot of log, so large restores are slow. PITR improves RPO but can hurt RTO, the time you are down. More frequent full backups shorten the replay.

**Mind the window:** If corruption is discovered after the retention window has passed, PITR cannot reach back far enough.

quiz.q: Your 5 TB database has weekly full backups plus PITR. A bad migration runs six days after the last full. Why might recovery take far longer than restoring the full backup alone?
